title: The Praetorian Guard
lead: The emperor's soldiers stationed at Rome, who in AD 68 and 69 helped make and unmake emperors. Paul writes that his chains had become known to the whole praetorium (Philippians 1:13), a word that in Rome may mean this guard.

sections.b: Wikipedia traces the Guard to Augustus, who kept it as his bodyguard under a prefect, and says Sejanus joined the cohorts into one camp at Rome under Tiberius. It reports that Claudius was the first emperor the Guard proclaimed (AD 41) and that a donative, a gift of money, was expected from each new emperor. Tacitus shows the system at work in 69: the Guard was promised a bonus in Galba's name that never came (1:5); Otho bought it with small gifts and a few agents (1:24-25); it chose its own prefects after Galba's death (1:46); and a night alarm before Otho left Rome nearly brought it to attack the Senate (1:80-82). The Praetorian prefect in Book 1 is Cornelius Laco (1:13).
sections.refs: Histories of Tacitus 1:5; Histories of Tacitus 1:13; Histories of Tacitus 1:24-28; Histories of Tacitus 1:80-82

sections.b: The Greek praitorion (from Latin) is Pilate's headquarters in Mark 15:16, Herod's palace at Caesarea in Acts 23:35, and in Philippians 1:13 either the guard or a headquarters in Rome. Paul in Rome was given permission to stay on his own, along with the soldier assigned to guard him (Acts 28:16). Philippians 4:22 sends greetings from "those who belong to Caesar's household".
